question.text:
Find a $2 \times 2$ matrix $F$ that has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=4$ and $\lambda_2=-2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

\[ \mathbf{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}= \{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $F,$ then $F$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $F=PDP^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $F,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order: \[ F= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{v}_1 & \mathbf{v}_2 \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix}}_{P} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 \\ \end{bmatrix}}_{D} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{v}_1 & \mathbf{v}_2 \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix}^{-1}}_{P^{-1}} \]

Let $P = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 \end{bmatrix}.$ Then,

\begin{align*} P^{-1} &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{-1} \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -5 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

\begin{align} F &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -10 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -26 & -30 \\ 24 & 28 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

question.explanation:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $M.$

\[ M= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}}_P \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2} \end{bmatrix}}_D \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}^{-1}}_{P^{-1}} \]

So, since $M=PDP^{-1}$, we can compute $M^k$ by using the formula \[ M^{k} = PD^{k}P^{-1}. \]

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get \[ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

\[ \begin {align*} M^{16} &= PD^{16}P^{-1}\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2} \end{bmatrix}^{16} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \big(\sqrt[8]{2}\big)^{16} & 0 \\ 0 & \big(\sqrt[4]{2}\big)^{16} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} {2}^2 & 0 \\ 0 &2^{4} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 16 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 48 \\ 4 & 32 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -32 & 72 \\ -24 & 52 \end{bmatrix} \end {align*} \]

question.text:
Find a $2 \times 2$ matrix $G$ that has eigenvalue $\lambda_1=6$ and $\lambda_2=8,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

\[ \mathbf{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}= \{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $G,$ then $G$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $G=PDP^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $G,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

\[ G= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{v}_1 & \mathbf{v}_2 \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix}}_{P} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 \\ \end{bmatrix}}_{D} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{v}_1 & \mathbf{v}_2 \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix}^{-1}}_{P^{-1}} \]

Let $P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{bmatrix}.$ Then,

\begin{align*} P^{-1} &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac 11\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

\begin{align} G &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 12 & 24 \\ 18 & 40 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -12 & 12 \\ -30 & 26 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

question.explanation:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

\[ A= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}}_P \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}}_D \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}^{-1}}_{P^{-1}} \]

So, since $A=PDP^{-1}$, we can compute $A^k$ by using the formula \[ A^{k} = PD^{k}P^{-1}. \]

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get \[ \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}^{-1}= \dfrac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix} -6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

\[ \begin {align*} A^{69} &= PD^{69}P^{-1}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}^{69} \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}^{-1}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1^{69} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{69} \end{bmatrix} \left( \dfrac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix} -6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \dfrac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \end {align*} \]

question.text:
Find a $2 \times 2$ matrix $S$ that has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=1,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

\[ \mathbf{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}= \{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $S,$ then $S$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $S=PDP^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $S,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

\[ S= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{v}_1 & \mathbf{v}_2 \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix}}_{P} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 \\ \end{bmatrix}}_{D} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{v}_1 & \mathbf{v}_2 \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix}^{-1}}_{P^{-1}} \]

Let $P = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Then,

\begin{align*} P^{-1} &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

\begin{align} S &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 18 & 1 \\ 15 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 13 & -12 \\ 10 & -9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}
